a privacy‑preserving strategy

Abstract
The rapid expansion of IoT devices has introduced significant cybersecurity risks, as attackers increasingly exploit these 
networks’ vulnerabilities. To counter this threat, this paper presents the Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence System (PEIoT-
DS), a novel solution that emphasises data privacy while delivering high-performance intrusion detection. PEIoT-DS use 
federated learning to create a comprehensive intrusion detection model without necessitating the transmission of raw 
data to a central server. IoT devices only contribute model updates, which are then combined to improve the global 
model. While allowing devices to benefit from the network’s collective insights, this decentralised learning methodol-
ogy safeguards data privacy. Using a real-world IoT dataset and two popular federated learning algorithms—Federated 
Average and Federated Average with Momentum—the study assesses the effectiveness of PEIoT-DS. The findings show 
that, in comparison to Federated Average, Federated Average with Momentum produces faster convergence and better 
intrusion detection accuracy. Our PEIoT-DS approach offers a reliable intrusion detection system for IoT networks while 
maintaining privacy.
Article highlights

detection framework that enables distributed IoTdevices to collaboratively identify cyber threats withoutsharing 
raw data. The approach ensures compliance withdata protection regulations and minimises the risk of dataexposure 
during the training process.
•	 Enhanced detection efficiency and accuracy: By leveraginglocal training on edge devices and securely aggregating-
model updates, the proposed method significantlyimproves the speed and accuracy of threat detection. Itadapts to 
device-specific data distributions while contributingto a robust global model, achieving high detectionperformance 
with minimal latency.
•	 Scalability and real-world applicability in IoT environments:The framework demonstrates strong scalabilityand 
effectiveness when tested on diverse realworldIoT datasets. It addresses the challenges of limitedbandwidth and 
computational resources by reducing communicationoverhead, making it suitable for deploymentin large-scale, 
heterogeneous IoT networks.

1  Introduction
The rapid adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has transformed connectivity and innovation, spanning from 
everyday gadgets to industrial sensors. These devices facilitate seamless data exchange, automation, and real-time 
monitoring across various sectors. Despite the benefits of IoT connectivity, the interdependent nature of IoT devices 
introduces significant security vulnerabilities–particularly those that compromise data integrity, confidentiality, and 
availability [1]. Due to their limited processing power and constrained energy capacity, traditional security mechanisms 
are often inadequate for IoT environments. This highlights the urgent need for robust and lightweight intrusion detec-
tion systems capable of protecting sensitive information and ensuring operational continuity.
Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a critical role in analysing network traffic to detect unauthorised activities. 
Among them, anomaly-based IDS are particularly effective, as they identify deviations from expected behaviour by 
comparing network activity against predefined patterns. Leveraging machine learning, these systems enable real-time 
threat detection and rapid response. However, conventional IDS typically rely on centralised data processing, which 
introduces substantial privacy and communication concerns [2].
Federated Learning (FL) addresses these limitations by enabling decentralised model training while retaining data on 
local devices. This approach not only enhances privacy by preventing raw data transmission but also reduces the risks 
associated with data leakage [2, 3].
In response to these challenges, we propose an innovative, IoT-specific Intrusion Detection System (IDS) that leverages 
Federated Learning. FL offers a practical solution to the trade-off between intrusion detection performance and data 
privacy by allowing IoT devices to collaboratively train a global model while keeping their data local. In this work, we 
present the design and implementation of the Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence System (PEIoT-DS), a federated learning-
based IDS that delivers effective intrusion detection while preserving user privacy.
We detail the system architecture, explain the federated learning workflow, and provide comprehensive experimental 
evaluations using real-world IoT datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability of PEIoT-
DS across diverse IoT environments. Additionally, we explore the privacy and security implications of our framework, 
contributing to the growing body of research on secure and privacy-aware IoT systems.
Our research evaluates two key federated learning aggregation techniques, Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and Fed-
erated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM), within the PEIoT-DS framework. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) [3] is a 
widely used method for aggregating local models trained independently by distributed nodes. Federated Averaging 
with Momentum ( FedAvgM) [4] enhances FedAvg by incorporating momentum, accelerating convergence, and effec-
tively handling data heterogeneity. These techniques enable IoT devices to collaboratively enhance a shared intrusion 
detection model while preserving data privacy. FedAvg involves independent local training on IoT devices, with model 
updates averaged by a central server to create a global model. However, FedAvg can be sensitive to variations in local 
datasets. FedAvgM addresses this by incorporating momentum, accelerating convergence, and providing smoother 
model updates, often outperforming FedAvg.
Our primary objective was to assess the effectiveness of federated learning in developing Intrusion Detection Systems 
(IDS) using the N-BaIoT dataset, a crucial resource for IoT intrusion detection research  [5]. This dataset includes nine 
subdatasets from various IoT devices. We implemented a horizontal federated learning architecture, using both FedAvg 
and FedAvgM with random client selection in each training round. Our empirical findings demonstrate FedAvgM’s supe-
riority over FedAvg in accuracy and convergence speed, particularly in privacy-sensitive scenarios. Federated learning 
proved effective in strengthening our IDS solution while ensuring data privacy, achieving an accuracy rate of 95.05% 
and lower loss rates compared to traditional deep learning models. FedAvgM also exhibited shorter testing times and 
better handling of data heterogeneity across all nine devices.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
•	 We investigated and experimentally applied two key federated learning aggregation techniques, FedAvg and FedAvgM, 
central to the development of the Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence System (PEIoT-DS).

2  Related work
Federated learning (FL) has gained attention as a promising method for intrusion detection across various network envi-
ronments, offering a way to share knowledge among users while protecting data privacy. McMahan et al. [3] introduced 
FedAvg, a pioneering algorithm that allows for the training of a global model without requiring clients to upload their 
data to a cecentralisederver. Federated Edge Learning (FEEL) shares similarities with FL but operates with the server 
located at the network edge. Mills et al. [6] proposed CE-FedAvg, an opoptimisedersion of FedAvg, which reduces the 
number of communication rounds needed for desired accuracy. Experiments with CE-FedAvg on the MNIST and CIFAR-
10 datasets in an edge setting showed faster convergence compared to FedAvg.
Recent research by Xie et al. in A Survey on Vulnerability of Federated Learning: A Learning Algorithm Perspective dem-
onstrates that model inversion attacks can extract sensitive training data from shared model updates, highlighting 
the limitations of federated learning (FL) in ensuring privacy. This underscores the critical need to integrate additional 
privacy-preserving mechanisms, such as differential privacy and secure aggregation, into FL frameworks [7].
The use of IoT in agriculture (Agri-IoT) is growing, but these networks are prone to vulnerabilities due to poor design 
and implementation [8]. Ferrag et al. [9] developed a deep learning-based Intrusion Detection System (IDS) to combat 
DDoS attacks in Agriculture 4.0, demonstrating effectiveness on the CIC-DDoS2019 and TON_IoT datasets. In another 
study [10], they introduced RDTIDS, a hierarchical IDS combining various classifiers like REP tree and JRip, achieving high 
detection rates with low false alarms on CICIDS2017 and BoT-IoT datasets.
While blockchain-IDS integration shows potential, it often requires centralised data for training, raising privacy con-
cerns. Traditional machine learning (ML)-based IDS require significant data, but centralizing this data can lead to privacy 
and latency issues, especially in complex environments [11]. FL addresses these concerns by preserving data privacy, 
maintaining model accuracy, and reducing communication costs [3]. FL has been applied to IDS with deep learning; for 
instance, Preuveneers et al. [11] explored a federated IDS using a deep learning model combined with blockchain for 
transparency. However, the simplicity of the neural network in their study limits the broader applicability, and customi-
sation of FedAvg is necessary for optimal performance.
Rahman et al. [12] developed an FL-based IDS for IoT, achieving about 83.09% accuracy, comparable to centralised 
models, using the NSL-KDD dataset. However, the dataset’s age may limit its relevance due to the emergence of new 
cyber threats. Nguyen et al. [13] introduced DÏOT, an FL-based IDS for IoT that automatically adapts to different device 
types. It demonstrated a 95.6% attack detection rate within 257 ms and minimal false alarms during tests on devices 
infected with Mirai malware.
3  Framework
Within the framework of our PEIoT-DS, FL functions as a privacy-centric machine learning paradigm designed to address 
the specific challenges of IoT environments. PEIoT-DS enables multiple IoT devices to collaboratively train a shared 
machine learning model while ensuring the privacy of each device’s data. In this framework, each IoT device indepen-
dently trains a local model using its own dataset, ensuring that sensitive data remains on the device, thereby mitigating

without ever sharing raw data.
The core of this collaborative process is the aggregation of these model updates as illustrated in Fig. 1. A central server 
orchestrates the federated learning process by collecting and aggregating the updates to construct a global machine 
learning model. This global model integrates the knowledge and insights from all participating IoT devices, resulting in 
a more robust and accurate intrusion detection system. Once the global model is built, it is distributed back to all the 
IoT devices in the PEIoT-DS framework, enabling real-time intrusion detection that harnesses the collective intelligence 
of the IoT network while maintaining data privacy and security.
3.1  Architecture of PEIoT‑DS
The architecture of the PEIoT-DS is based on the principles of federated learning and privacy-preserving machine learn-
ing, structured around three key components: 
(1)	 Central aggregator: The central aggregator in PEIoT-DS coordinates the training and deployment of the global 
intrusion detection model, updating it with local training results from IoT devices. It ensures data privacy by not 
receiving or storing raw data.
(2)	 IoT devices:Each IoT device in the PEIoT-DS network refines the intrusion detection model through local training 
using its own data. Instead of sending raw data, the device sends model updates to the central aggregator, ensuring 
that sensitive information remains secure on the device, preserving privacy..

3.2  Building the model
The federated learning approach within PEIoT-DS follows a coordinated, horizontal strategy, enabling IoT devices to 
collaboratively enhance a shared intrusion detection model without compromising data ownership. The essential 
steps in this process are as follows:

(1)	 Model initialisation: A global intrusion detection model is initially constructed by a central aggregator. This initial 
model serves as a foundational reference point and is distributed to all participating IoT devices.
(2)	 Localised Training: Each participating IoT device independently trains a local model based on its own dataset. As 
training occurs solely on-device, private data remains secure and confidential, never transmitted externally.
(3)	 Transmission of model updates: Following local training, each IoT device produces updates representing adjust-
ments to model parameters. These parameter modifications, reflecting locally learned patterns, are securely sent 
to the central aggregator without sharing any raw data.
(4)	 Model aggregation: The central aggregator collects updates from each IoT device and merges them to enhance the 
global intrusion detection model. Aggregation algorithms, such as Federated Averaging or momentum-enhanced 
variants, facilitate efficient integration of these distributed updates.
(5)	 Distribution of refined global model: The improved global model, incorporating insights from all contributing 
devices, is redistributed back to the IoT devices. This updated model forms the basis for subsequent rounds of 
localised training.
(6)	 Continuous iterations: The process repeatedly cycles through local training, model update transmission, and aggre-
gation. Each iteration progressively refines the global intrusion detection model, increasing its capability to accu-
rately identify security threats.
(7)	 Threshold-based intrusion detection: IoT devices employ the refined global model to monitor incoming network 
data. Deviations from expected behavioural patterns, as determined by established anomaly thresholds, trigger 
alerts indicating potential intrusions.
(8)	 Alerting and threat mitigation: Upon detecting anomalies, IoT devices immediately respond by generating alerts, 
activating defensive mechanisms, or notifying system administrators. Such prompt actions enable timely mitigation 
of detected threats.
Through its structured, iterative federated learning procedure, PEIoT-DS leverages collective device intelligence to con-
tinually advance the performance and accuracy of its intrusion detection capabilities. Simultaneously, this approach 
robustly preserves data privacy and adapts dynamically to emerging security challenges in diverse IoT scenarios.
3.3  IoT defence system with privacy enhancement (PEIoT‑DS)
The IoT Defence System with Privacy Enhancement (PEIoT-DS) is developed to tackle two major concerns in IoT security: 
safeguarding data privacy and enhancing the accuracy of intrusion detection. By combining federated learning with 
strong security mechanisms, PEIoT-DS offers a flexible and scalable solution suited for real-world IoT environments. This 
subsection outlines the core design aspects of the system, emphasizing its approach to data labeling, integrated security 
techniques, and deployment-focused improvements.
Strategy for local data labelling: Precise labelling of training data is fundamental for effective supervised intrusion 
detection. PEIoT-DS implements a layered strategy to ensure dependable label generation. During the initial setup, the 
system analyzes logs, device configurations, and past traffic data to build a preliminary labelled dataset. Network flows 
that align with standard behaviour are marked as "benign," whereas those matching known malicious signatures are 
classified as "malicious."
To complement this process, the system employs heuristic-based algorithms to detect and label unusual or suspicious 
activity. While such heuristic labels may occasionally lack precision, they serve as a valuable starting point for refining 
detection accuracy. To address the limited availability of labelled data on local devices, PEIoT-DS incorporates transfer 
learning. Through this approach, a globally trained model assists in labeling local data with high certainty, effectively 
reducing the manual effort required and accelerating the training process.
Securing the local training process: Given the inherent vulnerabilities of IoT devices, PEIoT-DS integrates robust mecha-
nisms to safeguard the local training process. Secure Multiparty Computation (SMPC) techniques are incorporated to 
ensure that model updates transmitted between devices and the aggregator remain secure and encrypted [14]. Fur-
thermore, differential privacy techniques are applied, introducing carefully calibrated noise into local model updates. 
This preserves the confidentiality of individual data points while retaining the accuracy of the aggregated global model. 
Additionally, Byzantine-resilient algorithms are implemented [15, 16], designed specifically to identify and exclude mali-
cious updates from compromised IoT devices, ensuring that the global model remains trustworthy and robust against 
adversarial manipulation.

Improvements for real-world implementation: To ensure effective deployment across diverse IoT environments, PEIoT-
DS incorporates several enhancements that optimise system performance and adaptability. High-confidence data sample 
prioritisation during local training is one example of this improvement. By focusing on samples with higher classification 
certainty, the system minimises the influence of noisy or potentially mislabelled data, which in turn accelerates conver-
gence and improves model reliability.
Furthermore, to strengthen the quality of training data, PEIoT-DS periodically incorporates externally labelled datasets 
from trusted centralised sources, such as Security Operations Centres (SOCs). These curated datasets help enrich the 
local data pools, allowing devices to benefit from expert-reviewed examples that may not be observable in their native 
environments. This hybrid approach ensures that the federated model remains robust against a wide variety of threat 
scenarios.
To maintain responsiveness in dynamic IoT contexts, the system integrates a centralised performance monitoring 
module. This module evaluates the performance of the global model on an ongoing basis and relays actionable feedback 
to participating edge devices. This continuous feedback loop enables rapid model adjustments in response to newly 
emerging threats, shifts in data distribution, or changing operational conditions, ensuring that PEIoT-DS remains adap-
tive and effective.
For robust and reproducible federated learning, PEIoT-DS implements two widely adopted algorithms: Federated 
Averaging (FedAvg) and Federated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM). FedAvg, introduced by McMahan et al. [3], is 
known for its ability to balance communication efficiency and model accuracy in decentralised learning environments. 
FedAvgM, an enhanced variant proposed by Hsu et al. [4], incorporates momentum-based updates to accelerate conver-
gence and improve stability, especially in heterogeneous settings with non-IID (non-independent and identically distrib-
uted) data. Both algorithms were developed and implemented using PyTorch, with FedAvgM’s momentum mechanism 
playing a key role in stabilising learning processes and enhancing overall system performance.
These practical improvements collectively contribute to the scalability, adaptability, and resilience of PEIoT-DS, posi-
tioning it as a viable solution for privacy-preserving intrusion detection in complex IoT ecosystems.
4  Aggregation process
To enhance the collective intelligence of IoT devices for effective intrusion detection, the Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence 
System (PEIoT-DS) incorporates a robust aggregation mechanism. This mechanism is central to federated learning and is 
responsible for synthesising knowledge gained from distributed local models into a unified, global intrusion detection 
system. The aggregation process in PEIoT-DS is built upon two principal techniques: Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and 
Federated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM), each contributing to improved learning efficiency, convergence, and 
scalability in heterogeneous IoT environments.
4.1  Federated aggregation
Federated aggregation is a cooperative and decentralised learning technique that empowers IoT devices to collabora-
tively refine a global intrusion detection model without exchanging raw data. Each IoT device trains its local model using 
its unique, private dataset, thereby capturing contextual patterns specific to its environment. Following local training, 
the devices transmit only the learned model parameters (e.g., weights and biases) to a central aggregator server via 
secure communication protocols.
The central server performs aggregation by combining the received model updates into a unified global model, 
effectively leveraging the diversity of localised experiences. This process ensures that the global intrusion detection 
system benefits from a broad spectrum of network behaviours and threat patterns encountered across different devices.
The global model thus formed embodies the collective intelligence of all participating nodes. It evolves iteratively 
through multiple training rounds, with each round incorporating updated insights from a subset of devices. This iterative 
feedback loop enhances the model’s adaptability to emerging cyber threats and supports continuous learning without 
compromising individual data privacy.
Federated averaging (FedAvg) is the foundational aggregation algorithm used in this process. Introduced by McMahan 
et al. [3], FedAvg allows each participating device to perform several local training iterations before sending updates to 
the server, significantly reducing communication frequency and bandwidth consumption. The algorithm relies on three 
critical hyperparameters that influence the training dynamics:

•	 C (Client Fraction): Determines the proportion of available IoT devices selected to participate in each federated train-
ing round. This controls the level of parallelism and diversity in the learning process.
•	 E (Local Epochs): Indicates the number of complete passes each device makes over its local dataset during one train-
ing round. Higher values allow deeper local learning but may introduce variability across devices with non-IID data.
•	 B (Minibatch Size): Defines the number of data samples processed per gradient update during local training. This 
impacts both the training speed and generalization performance of the model.
By carefully tuning these parameters, FedAvg achieves a balance between local computation and global communication 
efficiency, making it highly suitable for resource-constrained IoT environments. The ability to reduce synchronization 
frequency while maintaining convergence ensures that the PEIoT-DS can scale across large networks with minimal over-
head. In subsequent sections, we describe how the FedAvgM extension further enhances this process by incorporating 
momentum-based updates, which improve training stability and convergence speed in highly heterogeneous settings.
However, it has been observed that FedAvg can struggle with convergence in scenarios where data distribution across 
devices is non-uniform or non-identical. This limitation highlights the importance of carefully managing the aggregation 
process to ensure robust model performance across diverse and heterogeneous IoT environments.

4.2  Federated averaging with momentum aggregation

of IoT IDS. This method extends the conventional Federated Averaging approach by incorporating a momentum term

cal updates from IoT devices, imparting a momentum-enhanced characteristic to the model aggregation. This approach 
allows for smoother and faster convergence of the global intrusion detection model, even in the presence of noisy or 
diverse client updates, significantly improving both accuracy and efficiency. The update rule is expressed as:

5  Experimental setup
In order to evaluate the effectiveness, computational efficiency, and privacy-preserving capabilities of the proposed 
Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence System (PEIoT-DS) in realistic IoT environments, this section outlines the experimental 
design and implementation setup.
The evaluation was conducted within a simulated federated learning environment, comprising a centralized aggrega-
tion server and a network of virtualized IoT client devices. This setup was carefully designed to replicate the constraints 
and conditions typically found in real-world IoT deployments.
Each IoT client was configured to emulate the limited computational and memory capacities of edge devices com-
monly used in IoT networks. Specifically, each client was deployed on a virtual machine (VM) provisioned with 2 virtual 
CPUs (vCPUs) and 4 GB of RAM, closely representing the hardware characteristics of low-power embedded systems.
Conversely, the central aggregator was hosted on a high-performance computing node equipped with an Intel Core 
i7 processor, 32 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 3060 GPU. This server was responsible for orchestrating the federated 
learning workflow, aggregating model updates from clients, evaluating global model performance, and managing the 
feedback loop to participating devices.
The PEIoT-DS framework was implemented using Python 3.9 and PyTorch 1.13. A custom federated learning simulation 
platform was developed to support distributed training across client devices. This platform allowed experimentation 
with both Federated Averaging (FedAvg) and Federated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM) to assess convergence 
performance and stability across different data distributions.
To simulate privacy-preserving communication, Secure Multiparty Computation (SMPC) was integrated into the sys-
tem using the PySyft library. This enabled encryption and secure exchange of model parameters, ensuring that raw data 
remained local to each client throughout the learning process.
Furthermore, network communication between clients and the aggregator was configured to reflect secure and 
bandwidth-limited IoT network conditions. Latency and bandwidth constraints were artificially introduced to simulate 
the performance of wireless communication protocols such as LPWAN, Zigbee, or Wi-Fi typically found in IoT ecosystems.

The experimental design also included mechanisms to monitor system metrics such as training time, model conver-
gence rate, communication overhead, memory usage, and intrusion detection accuracy. These metrics were used to 
comprehensively assess the practicality and robustness of PEIoT-DS under varying conditions, including changes in client 
participation rates, data heterogeneity, and network stability. This setup provides a controlled yet realistic environment 
to validate the PEIoT-DS framework’s scalability and adaptability in a wide range of operational IoT contexts.
For training and evaluation, we used the N-BaIoT dataset, a publicly available and widely accepted benchmark for 
IoT network intrusion detection. The dataset comprises over 7 million traffic instances collected from nine different IoT 
devices, including smart cameras, door locks, and sensors. These devices were subjected to various botnet attacks such 
as Mirai, BASHLITE, and Gafgyt, which were executed in a controlled lab environment. Each traffic record is represented 
by 115 statistical features derived from packet-level behavior over specified time windows.
Prior to model training, the dataset underwent a standard preprocessing pipeline. This included Min-Max normaliza-
tion to scale feature values, one-hot encoding for multiclass attack labels, and the removal of redundant or constant 
features. The preprocessed data was divided into 70% for training and 30% for testing. To reflect realistic federated 
conditions, the dataset was partitioned in a non-identically distributed (non-IID) fashion among the nine simulated IoT 
clients, with each client receiving device-specific data exhibiting unique behavioral characteristics.
This experimental setup enabled us to assess the PEIoT-DS system under conditions that closely emulate real-world 
deployment, while also allowing controlled testing of its scalability, detection accuracy, and robustness to heterogeneity 
and resource constraints.
5.1  Dataset description
The N-BaIoT dataset [17] is a well-regarded benchmark specifically developed for designing and evaluating intrusion 
detection systems (IDS) in Internet of Things (IoT) environments. Created through a collaboration between researchers at 
the Universities of Cagliari and Pisa, the dataset captures realistic network traffic from a range of IoT devices—including 
smart cameras, door locks, and light bulbs—under both normal and malicious conditions.
To simulate real-world threats, the dataset includes 12 distinct attack scenarios based on actual IoT botnets such as 
Mirai, BASHLITE, and Gafgyt. These attacks were conducted in a controlled laboratory setting using real malware samples. 
Over the span of one week, approximately 9.2 GB of raw network traffic data was collected using specialized sniffing 
tools. The traffic was then preprocessed and meticulously labeled to distinguish between benign and malicious activity.
In total, the dataset comprises 7,062,606 traffic records, each represented by 115 statistical features. These features 
are systematically organized into three segments, separated by underscores:
•	 The first segment identifies the stream aggregation method used, such as "MI_dir," "HH," or "HpHp."
•	 The second segment ("L5" or "L3") indicates the time window of data aggregation–specifically the last 500 milliseconds 
or 1.5 s.
•	 The third segment provides statistical descriptors, including attributes like "weight," "mean," and "variance."
Thanks to its detailed structure and comprehensive coverage of various attack types, the N-BaIoT dataset offers a strong 
foundation for evaluating the performance, accuracy, and robustness of intrusion detection frameworks such as the 
proposed PEIoT-DS. Its realistic simulation of IoT network conditions makes it especially suitable for benchmarking 
privacy-preserving and distributed detection systems.

5.2  Results and evaluation
The performance of the proposed PEIoT-DS framework was thoroughly evaluated through a series of rigorous experi-
ments designed to assess both the system’s accuracy in detecting intrusions and its effectiveness in preserving data 
privacy in a federated learning context.
Figures 3 and 4 illustrate the accuracy progression of the Intrusion Detection System (IDS) models trained using FedAvg 
and FedAvgM, respectively, across 30 communication rounds. Both configurations show a consistent improvement in 
classification performance as training progresses, with FedAvg reaching a peak accuracy of approximately 94.05% and 
FedAvgM achieving a slightly higher accuracy of around 95.05% by the final round. These results confirm the capability 
of both aggregation methods to effectively train IDS models in a decentralized manner.
Notably, FedAvgM consistently outperforms FedAvg throughout the training process. Its faster convergence—reach-
ing the 90% accuracy threshold in only 17 rounds compared to 24 rounds with FedAvg—demonstrates the advantage of 
momentum in stabilizing training and accelerating learning. The smoother optimization dynamics provided by FedAvgM 
appear to enhance both training stability and the model’s generalization capabilities in non-IID settings commonly 
encountered in IoT environments.
In terms of detection reliability, FedAvgM also yields a lower false positive rate (FPR), reducing it to 3.9% compared to 
5.1% for FedAvg. This improvement is critical for real-world deployments, where minimizing false alarms ensures efficient 
use of security resources and improves user trust. Additionally, FedAvgM handles data heterogeneity more robustly, 
leading to more consistent local model updates across clients and fewer communication rounds overall.
The system’s efficiency was also assessed in terms of computational and communication overhead. On average, each 
IoT node required approximately 0.89 s to complete one local training epoch. The communication payload per round per 
client was about 320KB, including encrypted model updates, which were transmitted over simulated secure channels 
mimicking bandwidth-constrained IoT networks (Table 1).
A comparative evaluation of PEIoT-DS against existing intrusion detection solutions is presented in Table 2. The results 
confirm that PEIoT-DS delivers competitive or superior performance across multiple metrics–achieving high detection 
accuracy, strong privacy guarantees, reduced false positives, and efficient communication overhead. These characteristics

To provide further clarity on the trade-offs between privacy enhancements and system performance, we analyzed

Homomorphic encryption, although highly secure, imposes significant computational demands, potentially leading to 
increased latency and energy consumption in IoT devices with limited resources. These findings highlight the impor-

6  Discussion
The results from our experimental evaluation highlight the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed PEIoT-DS 
framework as a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient, and accurate intrusion detection system for IoT environ-
ments using federated learning.
The adoption of the Federated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM) technique significantly enhanced the overall 
system performance compared to the traditional FedAvg. Specifically, FedAvgM not only improved the peak detection 
accuracy (95.05% compared to 94.05%) but also demonstrated a faster convergence rate—achieving over 90% accuracy 
in just 17 rounds versus 24 rounds for FedAvg. This performance gain can be attributed to the momentum component, 
which stabilizes gradient updates and reduces oscillations, especially in environments characterized by non-identically 
distributed (non-IID) data. Such conditions are common in real-world IoT networks, where each edge device may observe 
a distinct subset of traffic behaviors based on its role and placement.
The improvement in the false positive rate (3.9% for FedAvgM vs. 5.1% for FedAvg) also reflects the model’s increased 
reliability. In intrusion detection systems, reducing false alarms is crucial, as high false positive rates may lead to alert 
fatigue and desensitization among system administrators, ultimately lowering the operational effectiveness of the secu-
rity infrastructure.
Moreover, the communication efficiency observed with FedAvgM has important implications. By reducing the num-
ber of communication rounds while maintaining high performance, PEIoT-DS minimizes bandwidth consumption—a 
critical requirement in resource-constrained IoT networks. Each client transmitted only  320KB of data per round, which

makes the framework viable for deployment on devices with limited network capacity. The lightweight architecture and 
short training times (averaging 0.89 s per local epoch) further reinforce the framework’s suitability for low-power edge 
computing environments.
Another core strength of PEIoT-DS lies in its integration of privacy-preserving mechanisms. By leveraging Secure 
Multiparty Computation (SMPC) and Differential Privacy (DP), the framework ensures that sensitive local data remains 
on the originating devices and that updates shared with the aggregator are encrypted or noise-obscured. This design 
not only meets compliance requirements for data protection (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) but also builds user trust in federated 
collaborative learning environments.
In comparison with other IDS solutions such as DÏoT, CE-FedAvg, Blockchain-IDS, and RDTIDS, our framework offers a 
more balanced approach by integrating strong privacy, real-time performance, and adaptability to heterogeneous data. 
Table 2 summarizes this comparative advantage across key features.
Despite these promising results, the current study has several limitations. First, the experiments were conducted in 
a simulated federated environment, which, although realistic, does not fully replicate the complexities of real-world 
deployment, such as unpredictable network latency, intermittent client availability, and hardware variability. Second, 
while we simulated privacy techniques, real deployment of SMPC and DP may introduce additional computational 
overhead, which needs to be quantified in future work. Third, the current implementation does not yet account for 
adversarial clients who may submit poisoned or misleading model updates. Although the use of FedAvgM contributes to 
model stability, more robust aggregation strategies such as Byzantine-resilient algorithms are needed to defend against 
targeted attacks in adversarial settings.
To address these limitations, future work will explore the deployment of PEIoT-DS on physical IoT hardware in a real-
world testbed to assess performance under practical constraints. We also plan to integrate lightweight Byzantine-resilient 
techniques and anomaly-aware aggregation strategies that can detect and neutralize malicious clients without signifi-
cantly increasing system complexity. Additionally, adaptive client selection methods and model personalization strate-
gies will be investigated to further enhance performance in diverse and dynamic IoT environments. PEIoT-DS presents a 
compelling and scalable architecture for secure and intelligent intrusion detection in federated IoT networks. Its strong 
privacy protection, real-time capability, and adaptability to resource-constrained devices make it an ideal candidate 
for next-generation distributed security systems in smart homes, industrial IoT, and critical infrastructure applications.
7  Conclusion and future work
This paper has introduced the PEIoT-DS, a novel system that leverages federated learning to maintain data privacy while 
delivering high accuracy in intrusion detection. We evaluated PEIoT-DS using the N-BaIoT dataset and demonstrated that 
it surpasses existing centralised and federated learning-based IDS approaches.
Our findings highlight the notable improvements in IoT security achieved through federated learning. Specifically, 
we have shown that:
•	 Federated learning enables high-accuracy intrusion detection while preserving data privacy.
•	 Federated Averaging with Momentum (FedAvgM) outperforms Federated Averaging (FedAvg), underscoring the 
significance of aggregation techniques in federated learning.
•	 Federated learning is effectively applicable to various IoT domains, including smart homes and industrial networks.
•	 The integration of a horizontal federated learning architecture, combined with average aggregation momentum and 
random client selection, can enhance the efficiency, fairness, and accuracy of federated learning-based IDS systems.
Our research emphasises the vital role of federated learning in advancing IoT security and provides a solid foundation 
for future exploration in this dynamic field. We believe that PEIoT-DS has the potential to transform IoT security manage-
ment, allowing organisations to better protect their devices and data against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.
Future research directions include expanding PEIoT-DS to detect a broader range of IoT attacks, exploring federated 
learning applications for other IoT security tasks such as anomaly detection and malware classification, and deploying 
PEIoT-DS in real-world IoT environments to assess its practical performance.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of IoT devices has introduced significant cybersecurity risks, as attackers increasingly exploit these networks’ vulnerabilities. To counter this threat, this paper presents the Privacy-Enhanced IoT Defence System (PEIoT- DS), a novel solution that emphasises data privacy while delivering high-performance intrusion detection. PEIoT-DS use federated learning to create a comprehensive intrusion detection model without necessitating the transmission of raw data to a central server. IoT devices only contribute model updates, which are then combined to improve the global model. While allowing devices to benefit from the network’s collective insights, this decentralised learning methodol- ogy safeguards data privacy. Using a real-world IoT dataset and two popular federated learning algorithms—Federated Average and Federated Average with Momentum—the study assesses the effectiveness of PEIoT-DS. The findings show that, in comparison to Federated Average, Federated Average with Momentum produces faster convergence and better intrusion detection accuracy. Our PEIoT-DS approach offers a reliable intrusion detection system for IoT networks while maintaining privacy. Article highlights • Privacy-centric intrusion detection: This study introducesa federated learning-based, privacy-preserving intrusion- detection framework that enables distributed IoTdevices to collaboratively identify cyber threats withoutsharing raw data. The approach ensures compliance withdata protection regulations and minimises the risk of dataexposure during the training process. • Enhanced detection efficiency and accuracy: By leveraginglocal training on edge devices and securely aggregating- model updates, the proposed method significantlyimproves the speed and accuracy of threat detection. Itadapts to device-specific data distributions while contributingto a robust global model, achieving high detectionperformance with minimal latency. • Scalability and real-world applicability in IoT environments:The framework demonstrates strong scalabilityand effectiveness when tested on diverse realworldIoT datasets.
